rv.q: It is a spectacular show, distilling the carnivalesque spirit of the book yet managing to control its many unruly parts and surfeit of imagination.
The show catches something of the oddity, excess and hidden terrors of modern London.
Raine’s production is hugely entertaining, bruising and tender.
As an exercise in collaboration and in its great arcing ambition, it’s pretty glorious.

The result, a tumbling odyssey through the city, is certainly baggy and patchy, but it has a generous warmth and wit and is underpinned by a keen sense that those who really keep the city going are often unsung.
It feels like a fitting tribute as well as a powerful way to conclude a heartfelt project.
She makes it seem like faith: mysterious, immutable and definite.
‘Stories’, Nina Raine’s follow up to her acclaimed play ‘Consent’, is an occasionally mercilessly witty but baggy exploration of the tales that society surrounds women with regarding motherhood.
But it just doesn’t hang together the way it should.
This is a flawed play and production, not a bad one.

A portrait of a childless, unattached woman on the verge of her forties desperately seeking impregnation, Stories finds her homing in again on a heavyweight issue and bringing to it a lightness of touch, but while she delivers a bundle of laughs, the balance is misjudged.
Unfortunately the very same could be said for Nina Raine’s play about Anna’s quest to conceive a child.
At the heart of this muddled and idiotic play is an attempt to parrot the orthodoxy that the wealth of Europe is the plunder of a superior culture in Africa.
This one’s a stinker – suitable only for theatrical rubber-neckers.

Oh and there are two blood-soaked men who have time-travelled from the Congo where, some years hence, Belgium’s King Leopold will rule over the genocide of 10million people. Unless, that is, the wily, clever Marjory can get there in time to stop it.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this anthology of London stories curated by James Graham. While some praise the ambition and standout contributions, others find it an uneven hodgepodge that doesn't fully cohere.
